hints: Start by reminding yourself what the four column headings mean - a monomer is a small single unit, a polymer is many monomers joined, and saccharides are all about sugars.
Pick out the two single sugars in Fig. 5.1. Both are monomers and monosaccharides, but they each build a different polysaccharide polymer.
Now look for the protein pair. One is a single amino acid and the other is a polypeptide chain made of many amino acids.
Look for the nucleic acid pair. One is a single nucleotide and the other is a long polynucleotide chain.

Remember each name must appear at least once, and some names belong in two columns at the same time - check that alpha-glucose, beta-glucose, glycine and thymine nucleotide are each in monomers and also in monosaccharides or paired with their polymer.
walkthrough:
Sort Small Units From Large Chains**
A monomer is a relatively small molecule that can join to others to form a polymer. A polymer is a large molecule made of many repeated monomers joined by covalent bonds. So scan the list for small versus large.

Pair The Sugars With Their Polysaccharides**
Alpha-glucose and beta-glucose are both hexose monosaccharides, so they go in both monomers and monosaccharides columns. Many alpha-glucose monomers join by glycosidic bonds to form glycogen, and many beta-glucose monomers join to form cellulose. So glycogen and cellulose go in both polymers and polysaccharides columns.

Pair The Protein And Nucleic Acid Building Blocks**
Glycine is an amino acid, so it is a monomer only. Many amino acids join by peptide bonds to form alpha-globin, which is a polypeptide polymer. Thymine nucleotide is a monomer, and many nucleotides join by phosphodiester bonds to form messenger RNA, which is a polynucleotide polymer.

Check Every Name Is Used**
All eight names appear at least once. Alpha-glucose, beta-glucose, glycine and thymine nucleotide appear as monomers, while messenger RNA, glycogen, cellulose and alpha-globin appear as polymers.

Final answer: monomers: thymine nucleotide, alpha-glucose, beta-glucose, glycine; polymers: messenger RNA, glycogen, cellulose, alpha-globin; monosaccharides: alpha-glucose, beta-glucose; polysaccharides: glycogen, cellulose.

hints: Picture a single phospholipid - one end is a phosphate head and the other end is two fatty acid tails. Think about which end mixes with water and which end avoids water.
Remember the cell membrane sits between two watery fluids - cytoplasm inside and tissue fluid outside. Think about which way the two layers of heads must face.
Now think about where the tails must end up if the heads are facing water on both sides, and what holds the tails together in the middle.
walkthrough:
See Phospholipids As Having Two Opposite Ends**
Each phospholipid has a phosphate head that is polar, so it is hydrophilic and attracts water. It also has two fatty acid hydrocarbon tails that are non-polar, so they are hydrophobic and repel water. This makes the whole molecule partly water-loving and partly water-fearing.

Heads Face Water On Both Sides**
In a cell, there is water on both sides of the membrane - cytoplasm inside and tissue fluid outside. So phospholipids arrange in two layers with the hydrophilic heads pointing outward to contact water on each side.

Tails Hide In The Middle To Form The Bilayer**
The hydrophobic tails point inward, away from water, meeting tail-to-tail in the centre. This creates a hydrophobic core in the middle of the bilayer, held together by hydrophobic interactions between tails, which forms a stable barrier to water-soluble substances.

Final answer: Phosphate head is hydrophilic / polar and fatty acid tails are hydrophobic / non-polar; heads face outward to watery cytoplasm and tissue fluid; tails face inward away from water forming a hydrophobic core stabilised by hydrophobic interactions.
